title: Thieves’ cant slang
content:
Insider jargon, previously known as cant, is designed to keep outsiders out.

The burglars in cartoons are often seen wearing a black mask over their eyes (like Robin in Batman but for a different reason) and carrying a bulging sack over their shoulders.

[Of course, the burglar’s sack was rarely bulging. A robber would have to have the perfect haul to get the right mix of value, density and weight. You can’t fit a chest of drawers in the sack, and that much gold would be impossible to carry. But I digress.]

The cant for this was ‘swag’, which comes from an old term for swaying or bulging. Sort of wishful thinking.

And thus we get to the swag of business promo and conference loot…

Establishing jargon is a key step in group identity. It’s rarely dictated from the top down, but permitting and celebrating it is a smart move if you’re looking for group cohesion.

# Walking May Improve Your Attention Span

One more reason to get those steps in

[JC](http://nautil.us/author/jake-currie)

By [Jake Currie](http://nautil.us/author/jake-currie)

6:00 PM CDT on October 19, 2026

[Add Nautilus to Google](https://google.com/preferences/source?q=nautil.us)

![Image 4](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/2026/10/shutterstock_2051774690.jpg?w=2880)

Walking is a great way to clear your head—or so anecdotes would have you believe. Now a new long-term study [published](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-74379-6) in _Scientific Reports_ is putting some intellectual heft behind this advice.

[Video 2](blob:http://nautil.us/c41cd772-44ca-4b7d-993e-45db1fa37dab)

Powered By

00:00/01:09

10

Share

Next

Stay

![Image 5](https://pl.primis.tech/live/liveView.php?&stnaInterval=0)![Image 6](https://pl.primis.tech/live/liveView.php?&stnaInterval=0)

Researchers from the Baylor College of Medicine uncovered the relationship by analyzing 14 years of health data from more than 3,000 adults aged 18 to 93 as part of the NIH’s All of Us Research Program. The team relied on daily step counts recorded by FitBits monitors, rather than self-reported daily activity (which tends to be less accurate). Additionally, the participants took cognitive assessments to measure their sustained attention, cognitive control (the ability to filter out distractions), delay discounting (the ability to delay gratification), and emotion recognition (the ability to read facial expressions).

**Read more: “**[**Here’s Why Our Walking Gets Slower as We Age**](https://nautil.us/heres-why-our-walking-gets-slower-as-we-age-1281837)**”**

Per the team’s analysis, people tended to cluster in three different groups according to their daily steps. Group A had the lowest activity levels, walking on average only 5,100 steps per day. Group B walked about 8,900 steps each day, and Group C was the most active, getting in roughly 14,200 steps per day.

[Subscribe to skip ads](http://nautil.us/products)Advertisement

So how were their brains?

After controlling for factors like age, education, and income, the team found that the two more active groups tended to perform better in cognitive tests than the least active group. Each additional 1,000 steps per day (relative to a person’s average steps) led to incremental improvements in sustained attention, cognitive control, and delay discounting (emotion recognition showed no association with activity).

Unfortunately, because the team only performed one cognitive assessment over the period, they can’t speak to how increasing or decreasing step count can alter our ability to stay on task or delay gratification. But it’s nice to know that those who get their steps in can reap mental rewards as well as physical ones. ![Image 7](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: Longevity Research Has a Bullshit Problem
content:
Debunking a case that is widely accepted by the scientific community is like seeing a piece of a movie set fall over: You realize in a moment that the saloon in the spaghetti western is not a two-­story building but a painted two-­dimensional prop made of plywood. You have the illusion of solidity in one moment, an incredulous feeling of having been tricked in the next, and after a stunned second you begin looking at the entire street thinking, “I bet that brothel’s made of cardboard.”

I had this feeling on a regular basis once I began investigating the world’s oldest people.

**Read more: “**[**The Longevity Skeptic**](https://nautil.us/the-longevity-skeptic-305806)**”**

Some cases required no effort at all. At one point, for example, the oldest woman in the United States was Adele Dunlap, a former smoker and occasional drinker. Adele kept insisting that the records had her age wrong. In a farcical, tragicomically weird end to her life, nobody believed her, and she was collectively rubbished for being unable to remember her real age. Despite consistently claiming for almost a decade that her paperwork was wrong, and that she was a decade younger than her documents suggested, Adele was duly informed by newspapers that she was mistaken about herself.

The academics knew better. A typical exchange ran thus: “Asked how it felt to be 113, Dunlap… looked her questioner in the eye and answered: ‘I’m 104.’” The reporter shot her down: “She’s not. The Los Angeles-­based Gerontology Research Group [GRG], which tracks supercentenarians, or people 110 and older, has validated her age.” Faced with a contradiction, Robert Young—director of the GRG, who certifies age records for the Guinness World Records—­told this woman on her deathbed that she was wrong and that she was certified as the oldest woman in the country.

The logic was bizarre. It also made a lie of the idea that errors in age records will be discarded if, under cross-­examination, any flaws are found in the biography of extremely old people. This woman spent her terminal years repeating on a loop that she was not the oldest woman in America. Nobody listened. The Obamas even sent her a birthday card to congratulate her on being 113. Adele Dunlap was a supercentenarian whether she liked it or not. She still is, on paper.

It’s worth pausing to look at the man behind the validation of cases like Dunlap’s before moving on.

Robert Young’s capacity for fair judgment—the thing that case validations rest on—should be unimpeachable. Instead, he holds some irregular opinions. His [master’s thesis](https://scholarworks.gsu.edu/items/20945cfd-a2a7-455c-a57f-587c5d3e979d) alone is enlightening. Some problems are simple, like the observation that “people who look young for their age live longer (citation needed)” [sic]. Others are more problematic. Young promotes resurrecting race science using what he calls the “biological superiority hypothesis,” which he supports despite it being not “politically correct,” because he “gained a better understanding of the myth of African-American longevity, mainly from the movies and P.T. Barnum.” He quotes Eddie Murphy’s comedy “Coming to America” as source material. He then suggests he can sense the thickness of Black people’s skin. Young goes on to surmise that African Americans may survive to remarkable ages because their “thick skin” protects their “internal organs.” His primary evidence is that there is “a saying in the black community, ‘black don’t crack.’”

Young even does some Olympics watching and finds that in the 2008 sprinting events,

_blacks took not just first, second, and third—no non-Africans can be seen on the track. . . . But so far, no research has demonstrated that the ability to run fast is greater for one race of people than another due to genetics. This is something that, perhaps due to political correctness, has not been studied._

Ignoring, of course, the studies of the Third Reich, which clung to similar reasoning when Jesse Owens destroyed them in athletics. Young then concludes that Africans may run faster because they had “to escape from wild animals but also other humans,” which also mixes in his constant confusion between physical fitness and Darwinian fitness.

This would all just constitute a lousy thesis that should never have passed examination—I am looking at you, Georgia State University—if it were not for Young’s ongoing importance in longevity research.

Young has validated roughly half of all extreme-age data, but his reach extends further. For example, he was also responsible for assembling the New England Centenarian Study, the “gold standard” clinical study on centenarians in the United States. To establish the study, Young decided who was and was not 100 years old. He then screened cases and played “key roles in subject recruitment, ascertainment of demographic data, and age validation.” His method was to gather cases by scrolling the internet for news stories and waiting for emails—unsolicited emails—about old people. Despite having no way of establishing the level of bias introduced, the study authors concluded that “ascertainment bias is likely minimal.” All of which boded poorly for the role of hidden biases in the GRG, where Young’s “preferences” might creep into the data he was assembling.

Failures like Dunlap’s were not isolated. They were part of a broader pattern that became impossible to ignore. Irma Borgoglio was one. She lived to 103 in the speck-­sized and pleasant Italian village of Bellavista di Trivero with her unemployed son, 63-­year-­old Pierangelo Bussolera. The pair had been quiet enough, though Borgoglio was a bit of a shut-­in, almost certainly as a result of her being over 100 and living at the top of several flights of stairs. The neighbors often saw her waving from her balcony at the top of the apartments. Some visitors had popped by, but Irma was in bed. After this happened a few times, and because everyone loved Irma, the local police decided to check on her.

When they arrived, Irma Borgoglio was upright in her kitchen. Pierangelo claimed she was unwell, but the 103-year-­old was as solid as ever. Indeed, she was even more solid than ever. She was frozen. Pierangelo had extracted his mother from the freezer and managed to get her “propped up in the kitchen” but had stumbled when he apparently tried to explain that she had just died minutes earlier.

It hardly took Inspector Holmes to deduce why she was frozen next to an empty freezer. Pierangelo had been unemployed and under financial pressure, and when his mother died, he seemingly panicked. Some arguing about money [had been overheard](https://www.thetimes.com/world/article/man-tried-to-defrost-his-dead-mother-when-police-called-c3fvdvs7t) by the neighbors, but it had “suddenly stopped in March.” Pierangelo, now over 60, had told people, “She’s not well, she needs to stay in bed for now,” which was sort of true, and then bought a chest freezer and dragged it to the top-floor apartment by himself. Later, [visitors had noticed](https://archivio.blitzquotidiano.it/cronaca-italia/pensioni-nascondeva-nel-congelatore-la-madre-103-anni-morta-da-6-mesi-e-ritirava-lassegno-2541814/) how strange it seemed to have a massive freezer for just two people, with so much stuff piled on the lid. Pierangelo collected his mother’s pension the whole time.

Cases like this are easy to dismiss as desperate, local, and faintly absurd outliers. But the same willingness to accept implausible stories scales remarkably well.

In 1979, the oldest person in the Guinness World Records was the [validated 137-­year-­old Charlie Smith](https://www.nytimes.com/1979/10/07/archives/charlie-smith-exslave-is-dead-believed-oldest-american-at-137-i.html), who had been “verified by Social Security officials who said they had turned up documents that showed Mr. Smith had been sold into slavery in New Orleans in 1859.” Opportunity had leaped on Charlie when he was picking fruit, and his [employer told him he had to get some kind of ID](https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-tampa-tribune-charlie-smitholdest/23261229/). The Social Security Administration found him an ID on file, promptly informed him he was 113 years old, and then lost the file. The old gasbag just went along with it and, hilariously, the entire nation bought the jibber-­jabber.

People believed Charlie no matter how big the tale. He said he was the last surviving American slave, last Union soldier of the American Civil War, and the first African American to be made a Freemason. (This was actually Prince Hall and 14 other anonymous African Americans in 1774, followed by literally thousands of other people, well before Charlie was said to have entered the United States in 1854.) He came from “Galina, Africa”: a port in Liberia that doesn’t exist, where he was apparently lured onto a slave ship by a “syrup tree” and an enslaver named Legree. He said he shot an innocent preacher in a packed church and the judge just let him go. Charlie also had many ever-changing jobs, always more glamorous than fruit-­picking, like lawman, bounty hunter, train robber, and honkytonk owner. He said he was a Texas cowboy who shot “bears and panthers… and lions,” an unusual addition to the local wildlife, and claimed he had ridden with Billy the Kid to successfully arrest the man who shot President Garfield. ([He did not.](https://thereader.mitpress.mit.edu/how-james-garfields-assassination-gave-birth-to-the-american-news-cycle/))

Charlie had other troubles with anachronisms too, like in 1975 when he said he was 144 but was supposed to be 132. Nobody seemed to care. Instead of criticism, Charlie was invited to the launch of Apollo 17 as a VIP, where he loudly informed Neil Armstrong, Dick Gordon, and everyone else in the shelter, “Ain’t nobody goin’ t’ no moon, you, me, or anybody else.” He was certain that the moon launch stuff was (ironically) all fake. As the rockets took off, he crossed to a studio audience with CBS and told Walter Cronkite “they ain’t goin’ there . . . ain’t nobody runnin’ on the moon” before confidently saying he arrested President Garfield’s assassin.

After seeing Charlie’s charisma, Ripley’s Believe It or Not! put him on national television and the BBC shot a documentary, with an amazingly posh British presenter throwing upper-class shade at all his tall tales. Charlie’s life was then dramatized in a PBS film that uncritically supported his claim that he rode with Jesse James, worked as a circus sideshow attraction, and chased Billy the Kid. Like Billy and Jesse James, they never took him alive, and Charlie Smith was memorialized in _The New York Times_ as “perhaps” age 137. The entire nation loved it. It was all pure bullshit. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: “It Feels Like Something Out of Science Fiction”: Astronomers Find First Green Star
content:
One day, our sun will collapse into a superdense object about the size of Earth—a white dwarf. While our sun is an orangish-yellow, the resulting white dwarf will be… white obviously, right? Not necessarily. According to a new [study](http://dx.doi.org/10.1093/rasti/rzag069) from the University of Warwick, white dwarfs actually come in a rainbow of different colors.

The color of most stars is a function of its temperature: red stars are the coolest, orange and yellow stars are hotter, and blue and white stars are the hottest of all. “Most stars, including most white dwarfs, behave like ‘perfect radiators,’ so their color is set almost entirely by temperature,” study author and astrophysicist Mark Hollands explained in a [statement](https://warwick.ac.uk/news/pressreleases/astronomers-reveal-true-colours-of-white-dwarf-stars/). “But nobody had really looked into what else might be possible for white dwarfs.”

**Read more: “[Did Astronomers Finally Witness a Black Hole Eat a White Dwarf for the First Time?](https://nautil.us/did-astronomers-finally-witness-a-black-hole-eat-a-white-dwarf-for-the-first-time-1268498)”**

Why would they be different colors?

Well, the atmosphere of the coolest white dwarf stars is roughly as dense as water (still millions of times denser than our sun’s atmosphere). At this density, heavier elements like carbon, calcium, and sodium can mingle with the helium, absorbing their own unique wavelengths of light. That means that the true color of white dwarfs (the color our eyes would perceive if we could glimpse them up close) can vary.

Because these stars are too far away for us to see, Hollands and a team of astrophysicists analyzed existing data on the stars’ spectra, or the breakdown of the different wavelengths of light they emit. By running these wavelengths through a model of human color vision, the team was able to determine what color they would appear to our eyes.

Color-accurate simulated images of white dwarfs. Top panels: Sirius B’s hot hydrogen atmosphere gives it a bluish tinge. The cooler WDJ1147-7449 has an orange glow. Two white dwarfs with convection envelopes surfacing carbon give them pink and red hues. Bottom panels: Calcium, magnesium, and sodium from rocky debris give these white dwarfs tones ranging from pale green to blue. _Credit: Mark Hollands/University of Warwick_

“It turns out these incredibly dense stars can produce colors nobody expected, and some of them genuinely surprised me,” Hollands said.

For example, the atmosphere of white dwarf WD J1330+6435, which has some rocky material from its planetary system, includes trace elements of calcium, lithium, and sodium. According to the team’s model, it would appear chartreuse green to our eyes—the first known green star ever identified.

“​​The traces of sodium in the atmosphere of this white dwarf absorb the orange part of the spectrum, leaving behind a ghostly green glow,” Hollands said. “Imagine standing on a planet and looking up at a green star. It feels like something out of science fiction.”

The team also discovered the pinkest star ever, WD J1011+2845. This white (or pink?) dwarf 48 light-years from Earth has a deep convection zone that lifts carbon up to the atmosphere, distorting its starlight and giving it an otherworldly deep salmon color.

Of course, the average color of white dwarfs is still plain old white. After crunching the numbers on 151 white dwarfs within 65 light-years of Earth, the researchers found only five with extraordinary coloring (two were yellow, and three were pink). The rest would appear to us to be a cool white color, like an LED bulb. Great for lighting a cosmic kitchen at night, but nothing to write home about. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: The Wildlife Photo of the Year May Break Your Heart
content:
One of the great things about wildlife photography is how it allows us to bear witness to the whole cycle of life. There’s perhaps no better example of this than the images celebrated in this year’s Wildlife Photographer of the Year Awards, put on by London’s Natural History Museum. They showcase adults caring for their young, animals looking for food and sheltering from storms, and wildlife just doing their level best to survive.

Below, you’ll find some of the best images given highly commended status this year, together with the overall winner: a particularly poignant shot captured in southern Africa.

The overall winner of the competition was “The Aftermath” by Italian photographer Federico Veronesi. The photo, taken in Namibia, documents a female African elephant carrying a dead calf—a rare glimpse of how these animals behave around death. _Credit: Federico Veronesi/Wildlife Photographer of the Year_

“Mutual Friends” by South African photographer Ernest Porter features a red-billed oxpecker cleaning its bill with the help of a rhino. These oxpeckers snack on insects on the skins of rhinos, and alert them to dangerous animals that may be approaching. _Credit: Ernest Porter/Wildlife Photographer of the Year_

This curious polar bear was captured by an underwater camera set up in the Arctic by Audun Rikardsen from Norway, in a photo called “Icy Window.” Seals make these breathing holes for surfacing, but it also leaves them vulnerable to polar bears looking for food. _Credit: Audun Rikardsen/Wildlife Photographer of the Year_

Prasenjeet Yadav, a molecular biologist turned National Geographic photographer from India, used a hidden camera trap in India’s Similipal Tiger Reserve to secure a shot of a rare black tiger. _Credit: Prasenjeet Yadav/Wildlife Photographer of the Year_

The name “Split-Second Escape” gives you an idea of what you’re looking at in this image by German photographer Jens Cullmann: A lunging African bullfrog thinks it’s about to chow down on an African babul butterfly, but the butterfly somehow manages to make its escape. _Credit: Jens Cullmann/Wildlife Photographer of the Year_

“Calm Amid the Storm” is very much a photo of two halves, showing a threatening storm approaching above the water and a school of bigeye trevally fish below the waves. The image was taken by Canadian Shane Gross, just off D’Arros Island in the Seychelles. _Credit: Shane Gross/Wildlife Photographer of the Year_

Jason Gulley is a geology professor and freelance photographer from the U.S., and his shot of a mother and a calf manatee navigating murky waters is entitled “Between Layers.” Every winter, thousands of manatees head to sources of warmer water to ensure their survival. _Credit: Jason Gulley/Wildlife Photographer of the Year_

A flock of red-billed quelea birds star in “Flock of Gold” by Hungarian Bence Máté, who says, “You could feel the rush of air from tens of thousands of wings beating in unison, even from [98 feet] away.” _Credit: Bence Máté/Wildlife Photographer of the Year_

“Herd Huddle” by David Lloyd, a wildlife photographer from New Zealand, shows a group of Asian elephants forming a protective circle around two calves. It was taken from a distance, just before the herd turned around and disappeared into the forest. _Credit: David Lloyd/Wildlife Photographer of the Year_

There was also recognition for younger photographers. Amelie Davis from the U.K. took the top award in the 10 years and under category for “Flight of the Bumblebee,” which was captured in southern England on an iPhone Davis borrowed from her dad. _Credit: Amelie Davis/Wildlife Photographer of the Year_

The award for the Young Wildlife Photographer of the Year went to Oscar Whitfield from Zimbabwe, who captured this dung beetle pushing a pellet of poop along the ground. Taken in Zambezi National Park, the photograph is called “Labor of Love.” _Credit: Oscar Whitfield/Wildlife Photographer of the Year_

title: Teen Girls Are Now More Likely to Vape Than Boys
content:
With the advent of e-cigarettes, millions of smokers gained a way to get their nicotine fix without many of the negative health effects of lighting tobacco on fire. Of course, because the technology is relatively new, there’s plenty we don’t know about any other adverse long-term effects. That’s one reason it’s particularly troubling that young people have adopted vaping, too. Now the latest data on youth vaping trends is out, and it’s showing some interesting gender differences.

In a letter [published](http://dx.doi.org/10.1001/jamapediatrics.2026.4918) today in _JAMA Pediatrics_, a team of researchers from the Medical University of South Carolina reports that vaping is on the rise among girls. It’s a bit puzzling. For decades, the reverse was true—more men and boys indulged in nicotine products than women. But according to data from the youth cohort for the Population Assessment of Tobacco and Health (PATH) study, girls have been more likely to vape than boys since 2021, with a wider gap in older teens.

**Read more: “[How Nicotine Disrupts the “Lung-Brain Axis”—And Could Lead to Dementia](https://nautil.us/how-nicotine-disrupts-the-lung-brain-axis-and-could-lead-to-dementia-1279711)”**

The new study is the first to capture vaping trends among those between the ages of 12 and 17 across a full decade, from 2014 through 2024, focusing on those who had an established habit. The data came from self-reported surveys, which means it’s likely the findings underestimate the magnitude of the problem.

“That makes this a pretty conservative estimate of use,” study author Brandon Sanford explained in a [statement](https://hollingscancercenter.musc.edu/content-hub/News/2026/10/19/girls-vaping-at-higher-rates-than-boys). “These aren’t youth who simply tried vaping once or twice. We’re talking about adolescents who are regularly using e-cigarettes now.”

Older teen girls (aged 15-17) saw the biggest rise in vaping with 4.9 percent of them reporting regular use in 2021 and 7.8 percent in 2024. By contrast, only 4.6 percent of boys in the same age cohort said they were regular users in 2024.

According to the team, the latest data show a drop in teen girls vaping, but the gender gap still persists and the reasons remain unclear. “We would love to look into some of the whys,” Sanford said. “Are there shifts in motivation to use, marketing, social influences or perceptions?”

Drilling down into data the researchers found some other interesting contours. Vaping was more common among boys from 2014 through 2018, then a spike in both genders in 2018 and 2019 erased the gender gap. According to the team, this surge coincides with the popularity of new products like JUUL e-cigarettes—slim, rechargeable devices that use disposable cartridges of nicotine-salts in glycerol and propylene glycol.

The good news is that the number of teens smoking combustible cigarettes has dropped precipitously. According to the data, less than half of 1 percent of both boys and girls were established smokers, something the team calls a “massive health win.”

Still, nicotine by itself carries its own negative health externalities. For adolescents, that includes addiction at a time when their brains are still developing. Vaping may be safer than smoking, but without long-term data we won’t know exactly what teens are risking by picking up the habit. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: How Our Brains Read Emotions in Other People
content:
When you walk into a room and instantly sense conflict brewing among a huddle of people, or a friend tells you, “I’m fine,” but you have a strong intuition that they are not, you’re reading an unspoken language. Your mind collects cues from dozens of tiny facial expressions in the eyes, the mouth, the nose, the smile, the gaze of the other person. You’re also listening to the sound of their voice: its pitch, timbre, brightness, and loudness, sighs or gasps, pauses between words.

Reading emotion in this way is inherently multisensory. It’s also essential to building and maintaining social relationships. We make these calculations about emotion dozens of times a day. But because different parts of the brain tend to read faces and voices, it hasn’t been clear how the brain integrates these different signals to decode what another person is feeling.

**Read more:**[**“How Emotions Connect Your Body and Brain”**](https://nautil.us/how-emotions-connect-your-body-and-brain-237725)

Recently, a team of scientists decided to try to map this process out in the gray matter. They invited 24 people to a hospital in Brussels and scanned them with fMRI while they watched and/or listened to 20 brief video clips of four different actors expressing five different emotions: disgust, fear, happiness, sadness, and neutrality. The emotional content of face and voice always matched. Then the team used pattern analysis to see which region of the brain carried information about which emotions.

They found that deciphering an emotion from faces and vocal cues isn’t a tidy process, or a series of isolated steps. Instead, the brain processes emotional data across a broad network of face- and voice-selective brain regions at once. Almost all of these regions rely on the same neural “signal” to carry emotional meaning, regardless of its sensory origin. The sole exception was the occipital face area, which used distinct patterns for voices and faces. Also, while combining vocal and facial cues changes how the brain responds, it doesn’t make the brain any better at deciphering the underlying emotion. The team published their [results](https://dx.doi.org/10.1523/JNEUROSCI.0366-26.2026) in the _Journal of Neuroscience_.

The authors propose that emotion processing is shared across networks rather than siloed because faces and voices typically provide complementary information about emotional meaning. Earlier work, they point out, suggests that “face and voice regions constitute interacting networks specialized for socially meaningful information rather than strictly unimodal sensory systems.” The findings are consistent with studies that [show](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/pdf/10.1080/02699931.2025.2478478) impairments in emotion recognition often [affect](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02699931.2025.2478478) a person’s ability to decode both facial and vocal expressions.

Still, faces may play the dominant role in the understanding of emotion. When participants were looking at faces only, information about the emotions they were detecting still showed up in areas of the brain that respond preferentially to voices. But the reverse was weaker. The authors suggest this is because facial expressions tend to be recognized more reliably than voices, and—according to earlier work—are more often used to detect the underlying emotion when face and voice conflict.

A couple of caveats: A few important areas of the brain, including the amygdala, which helps to process emotion, and certain face-selective regions, weren’t reflected in the data. Moreover, the number of participants in the study, and the number of faces and vocal cues they were tested on, were small, so more data is needed.

But if the findings hold up, they suggest that the unspoken language of emotion is pretty universal. The brain reads what we see and what we hear as a single tongue. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: Open Thread 456
content:
This is the weekly visible open thread. Post about anything you want, ask random questions, whatever. ACX has an unofficial [subreddit](https://www.reddit.com/r/slatestarcodex/), [Discord](https://discord.gg/RTKtdut), and [bulletin board](https://www.datasecretslox.com/index.php), and [in-person meetups around the world](https://www.lesswrong.com/community?filters%5B0%5D=SSC). Most content is free, some is subscriber only; you can subscribe **[here](https://astralcodexten.substack.com/subscribe?)**. Also:

**1:**Meetup changes in Rockville, Northampton, Eindhoven, Great Barrington, Cairo, Portland, and Sofia. [Check the post](https://www.astralcodexten.com/p/meetups-everywhere-2026-times-and) for more information.

**2:**The Boston ACX meetup group has finished their [Greater Boston general election voting guide](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1dxSeXrFKr89jXFCMjR6bb36pxKIaryKBbW-2xA3mwLc/edit?tab=t.j1hjhhyx35js#heading=h.magzwuj217kv). I may have more of these in the upcoming week. Still trying to figure out if we can do something for the Bay Area, but remember that SF mail-in ballot registration due date is end-of-day today (Monday), and that our main SF endorsement is **Scott Wiener**for Congress. We may have more later.

**3:** I’m continuing to work on modeling (and maybe one day automating) some parts of AI grantmaking (you can see previous efforts [here](https://forum.effectivealtruism.org/posts/E7pkeDruknpSa7j3i/results-of-an-informal-survey-on-ai-grantmaking)). I would once again like people who are well-versed in the AI/grantmaking worlds to take a survey on how much they value various things. This one involves assigning utility weights to ~80 different AI safety accomplishments. **[Take it here](https://forms.gle/dXDaN7jFrHidLZWaA)**. After you’ve taken that survey, if you still have more time/energy it would be extra helpful for my data collection if you would take [this alternate version](https://forms.gle/FTUsJeGWZjQSvdYA7), which asks you to predict how _I_ would answer the first survey (so I can separate out worldview differences from weight-choosing random noise).

**4:**Bay Area ACX meetup is scheduled for this coming Saturday, 10/24, 1 PM, at Mox in SF (1680 Mission St). I’ll probably make a post about it, but consider this an early heads-up.

**5:**Grantee and Manifold Markets co-founder Stephen Grugett announces his latest project: [MNX](https://mnx.fi/) is a real-money prediction market on AI. It lets people sell futures representing AI company stocks, bet on AI company revenues directly, and a few other things like Epoch Capabilities Index targets. Interestingly, despite the talk of Anthropic’s API falling from from $2T to $1.5T, both Polymarket and MNX still price it around $2T.

**6:**Friend of the blog Goodheart Labs is working on Common Notes, aka “Twitter Community Notes, but for everything”. They’re implementing it through a combination of AIs (who write most notes), users (who write others, and vote on which ones are helpful), and a browser extension (which makes the system show up on everything, including this blog). [Check it out, and install the browser extension, here.](https://commonnotes.net/)

title: Directed Culture Trials
content:
> Unless we find new ways to drive adaptation besides mass death and fragmentation, our civilizations may keep falling and rising indefinitely. I see 3 new ways: let capitalism [run](https://www.overcomingbias.com/p/capitalist-voluntary) most all life areas, run small groups [by](https://www.overcomingbias.com/p/toward-adaption-futures) speculative market estimates of future group adaptive success, or run big groups [by](https://www.overcomingbias.com/p/futarchy-futurism) such price estimates of achieving big goals in conflict with civilization collapse. All three ways rely on strong selection among market traders creating information that lets groups stay adaptive without their death or division. ([More](https://www.overcomingbias.com/p/five-slogans-re-cultural-drift))

Those are three plausible strategies to drive an effective governance process to promote cultural adaption. But effective processes must then induce the more specific activities and choices that would actually be effective at inducing healthy cultural evolution. And I haven’t said much about specifically what those would be. I’ve also [suggested](https://www.overcomingbias.com/p/culture-guiding-futarchy) that a good preparation for any of these approaches would be to get good at managing corporate cultural change. But I also haven’t said how exactly we could do that. So let me now say more about these.

It seems pretty clear to me that actual processes that induce healthy cultural evolution must involve a lot of cultural experimentation. But instead of only random large variations characteristic of simple Darwinian evolution, I expect it to look more like the directed trials commonly done in agricultural, medical, and product innovation, and in venture capital.

In our capitalist world today, we do have many different products and services that just directly compete for customer allegiance in a mostly wild uncontrolled free-for-all. But those competing options were themselves usually generated and honed via more directed processes. For example, new product ideas often go through five stages of directed testing and trials: concept testing, prototype testing, product testing, field trials, and market trials. Ventures invest in those early stages out of hopes that they might lead to success versions in the final free-for-all contests.

As “cults” are relatively insular groups following deviant cultures, this may involve the promotion and testing of varied cults. And as norms and morals are a big part of culture, this also implies directed trials of different moral norms. Of course this usually wouldn’t allow moral deviants to be much excused on the grounds that they have contributed to cultural experimentation. But yes, there would be some element of that. When their deviations are aligned enough with interesting dimensions and experiments, yes moral deviants may well be credited for their assistance. Oh brave new world of moral experimentation.

title: History of 20 Sources of Moral Authority
content:
Though three weeks ago I [outlined](https://www.overcomingbias.com/p/the-arc-of-moral-authority-from-tradition) a story of the long-term history of changes to moral authority, I decided to study this in a bit more detail. So I collected this list of 20 candidate sources of moral authority: Activist/interest group, Hereditary elite, Artist/musician/storyteller, Business-leader/employer, Famous, Civic-frat/clubs/assoc, Doctor/therapist, Family/elder, Peer/Community, Govt leader/org, Heart/Conscience, Law, Market prices, News/Media, Public intellectual, Priest/Church/Sacredtxt, Scholar/scientist, School/teacher, Tradition, Warrior/Military. Then I asked three [L](https://claude.ai/share/d8e48d94-6284-4bec-a222-ce771e20ac5a)[L](https://chatgpt.com/share/6acc2039-1440-83ea-a4d9-6f7afaf58cab)[M](https://grok.com/share/c2hhcmQtMw_dc559746-a2e8-4820-a95f-71c0d1a9b9bc)s to rate the strength of each source (wrt max 100) in each of the six time periods between the dates 5KBC, 1AD, 1400, 1750, 1910, 2000, 2026. Here are their medians, with peaks highlighted in red, sorted to show the time progression, and by strength:

[![Image 1](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!7OcT!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F9412684b-5be6-42aa-b85a-b5cbecb2faab_956x1130.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!7OcT!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F9412684b-5be6-42aa-b85a-b5cbecb2faab_956x1130.png)

Notice some patterns. The ancient and modern eras were pretty different, and each of these eras can be split into early and late versions, which have mildly different sources. The ancient world changed from early, when tradition, family, and community peaked, to later, when priests, aristocrats, and warriors peaked. The modern era changed from early, when states, law, scholars, schools, and public intellectuals peaked, to later when hearts, activists, celebrities, news, and medicine peaked. Community (via social media) has also peaked again in the late modern era. Civic clubs peaked in a very early modern period.

Note that most ancient sources are still important in the modern era; what changed was that the modern era added many more sources. Thus sources have become a lot less concentrated over time. In the first period there were only 6 sources >50, while in the last there were 12. Only once source, artist/musician/storyteller, didn’t change much in strength over history.

In my prior post I said that to fix cultural drift we will need to rely a lot more on speculative market prices as sources of moral authority, but I didn’t know how that could happen. Here we see that though business and market prices have been rising in strength over time, the are still rather weak. But at least the trend is hopeful.

Note that the recent change in modern era trends could be seen as maladaptive.

**Added 13Oct**: To check robustness, I redid with [5](https://chatgpt.com/share/6ace5748-9754-83ea-986e-2ba1760389e9)[L](https://claude.ai/share/d8e48d94-6284-4bec-a222-ce771e20ac5a)[L](https://grok.com/share/c2hhcmQtMw_de747e20-6d6f-4b69-be64-9eef3202d906)[M](http://click%20the%20link%20to%20view%20the%20conversation%20with%20kimi%20https//www.kimi.ai/share/1a13605f-5622-8ed3-8000-000013c234f8)[s](https://meta.ai/share/c/QSLBKqTNu5), & 9 time periods between these 10 dates: 12K BC, 5K BC,1200 BC, 400AD, 1200, 1650, 1875, 1975, 2000, 2026:

[![Image 2](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!E9tf!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F0bbfbceb-4450-447b-a5c5-349234574ed7_664x736.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!E9tf!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F0bbfbceb-4450-447b-a5c5-349234574ed7_664x736.png)

Late ancient peaks are now spread out, while early modern peak is sharp. Art is now U-shaped like peers.
